name: Webvan
one_liner: Online grocery store that built its own automated warehouses and delivery fleet
story: Webvan spent heavily on automated warehouses and its own trucks before proving demand, raising about $800M including a $375M IPO in 1999. It bought rival HomeGrocer for $1.2B in stock in 2000, but losses of roughly $830M forced it to shut down in June 2001 and lay off about 2,000 people.

name: HomeGrocer
one_liner: Seattle-area online grocery delivery service backed by Amazon
story: HomeGrocer ran online grocery delivery in the Pacific Northwest and went public in March 2000. Months later it was swallowed by rival Webvan in a stock deal valued at $1.2B, and that stock became worthless when Webvan collapsed in 2001.

name: Pets.com
one_liner: Online pet supply store famous for its sock-puppet mascot
story: Pets.com sold heavy, low-margin goods like pet food below cost and shipped them nationwide, spending big on Super Bowl-era advertising. It raised $82.5M in a February 2000 IPO at $11 a share, then announced its liquidation in November 2000, about 268 days later, with the stock at $0.19.

name: Kozmo.com
one_liner: Free one-hour bike-courier delivery of snacks, videos and convenience goods
story: Kozmo promised free delivery of small items like ice cream and DVDs within an hour, expanding to multiple US cities with about 1,100 staff. It raised about $280M, including $60M from Amazon, but small orders with no delivery fee never covered courier costs, and it shut down in April 2001 after a planned IPO was cancelled.

name: Urbanfetch
one_liner: Free one-hour delivery of electronics, books and snacks in New York and London
story: Urbanfetch competed head-on with Kozmo, offering free one-hour delivery in Manhattan and London. It closed its consumer delivery business in 2000 after merger talks with Kozmo collapsed, months before Kozmo itself shut down.

name: eToys.com
one_liner: Online toy retailer that briefly out-valued Toys R Us
story: eToys went public at $20 a share in 1999 and its stock hit about $85, implying a market value near $7.8B. Big warehouse build-outs and costly holiday seasons left it with about $247M in debt, and it filed for bankruptcy in early 2001; its brand later sold at auction for about $3.35M.

name: theglobe.com
one_liner: Early social network of user home pages and chat rooms
story: Founded by two Cornell students, theglobe.com set a record when its November 1998 IPO priced at $9 and closed its first day at $63.50, a roughly 606% jump. Ad revenue collapsed with the dot-com bust and it shut its social network in 2001, years before Facebook made the idea work.

name: Flooz.com
one_liner: Online gift currency spendable at partner retailers, advertised by Whoopi Goldberg
story: Flooz tried to create a private internet currency that people could gift and spend at partner merchants, backed by a Whoopi Goldberg ad campaign. Consumers never adopted it beyond gifting, and it folded in 2001 as dot-com funding dried up.

name: Napster
one_liner: Peer-to-peer MP3 file-sharing service
story: Napster let tens of millions of people swap MP3s for free, becoming one of the fastest-growing apps ever. Record labels sued for copyright infringement, a court injunction shut the service in 2001, and the company went bankrupt in 2002 with its brand sold off.

name: Iridium LLC
one_liner: 66-satellite constellation for global satellite phone calls
story: Motorola-backed Iridium spent about $5B launching a low-earth-orbit satellite network, but its bulky handsets cost thousands of dollars and calls several dollars a minute while cheap cell networks spread. It filed for bankruptcy in 1999, less than a year after launching service, and the satellites were sold for about $25M.

name: DoubleClick
one_liner: Ad-serving technology for online display advertising
story: DoubleClick built the ad-serving plumbing for early web publishers and went public in 1998. It survived the dot-com crash, was taken private in 2005, and was bought by Google for $3.1B in 2007, becoming the core of Google's display ad business.

name: Amazon
one_liner: Online bookstore that became the everything store
story: Amazon started selling books online in 1995 and went public in May 1997 at $18 a share, raising $54M at a valuation of about $438M. It raised more debt before the 2000 crash, survived while peers like eToys and Pets.com died, and became one of the world's most valuable companies.

name: eBay
one_liner: Online person-to-person auction marketplace
story: eBay started as AuctionWeb in 1995 and was profitable early because it never held inventory. Benchmark's $6.7M investment became one of the best venture returns of the era after eBay's 1998 IPO, and eBay later bought PayPal.

name: PayPal
one_liner: Send money by email, built on eBay's marketplace
story: Confinity and Elon Musk's X.com merged in 2000 to form PayPal, which grew virally on eBay with cash referral bonuses while fighting heavy fraud losses. It went public in early 2002 and was bought by eBay later that year for $1.5B.

name: Salesforce
one_liner: CRM delivered as a cloud subscription instead of installed software
story: Founded in 1999 at the peak of the dot-com bubble, Salesforce sold CRM software over the internet by subscription under a 'No Software' slogan. It survived the crash and raised $110M in a 2004 IPO, becoming the template for SaaS companies.

name: Homejoy
one_liner: Book a vetted home cleaner online in a few clicks
story: Homejoy used cheap first-clean promotions to expand fast across US cities, but customers and cleaners often left the platform after a booking, so retention never paid back acquisition costs. Facing lawsuits over whether its cleaners were contractors or employees and unable to raise a Series C, it shut down in July 2015 after raising about $40M.

name: Handy
one_liner: On-demand marketplace for home cleaning and handyman jobs
story: Handy competed directly with Homejoy in cleaning and handyman bookings and even held talks to buy it in 2015. It outlasted its rival and was acquired by ANGI Homeservices in October 2018; ANGI's filing valued the 8.6M shares it issued at $165.8M plus cash.

name: Sidecar
one_liner: Peer-to-peer ridesharing app that pioneered letting ordinary drivers give rides
story: Sidecar was among the first apps to let regular drivers offer rides, before Uber and Lyft adopted the model. Outspent by both rivals, it pivoted to deliveries, then shut down on December 31, 2015 after raising about $35M-$39M; GM bought its assets and hired about 20 staff for less than that amount.

name: Washio
one_liner: On-demand laundry and dry-cleaning pickup and delivery
story: Washio was one of the 'Uber for X' startups, picking up laundry by app and returning it cleaned. Delivery costs on low-ticket orders never worked out, and it shut down in August 2016 after raising about $17M.

name: Shyp
one_liner: App that picks up, packs and ships any item for you
story: Shyp sent couriers to collect items, packed them in a warehouse and shipped them via carriers, expanding to several cities at a $250M valuation. Consumer orders were too infrequent and costly to serve, a pivot to e-commerce returns came too late, and it shut down in March 2018 after raising about $62M.

name: Sprig
one_liner: App delivering chef-cooked meals from its own kitchens in under 20 minutes
story: Sprig owned everything from cooking to delivery, which made each meal expensive to produce as restaurant marketplaces like DoorDash and Uber Eats grew. Reportedly burning $850,000 a month and unable to find a buyer, it shut down in May 2017 after raising about $57M.

name: Munchery
one_liner: Delivery of chef-prepared meals cooked in central kitchens
story: Munchery cooked meals in its own kitchens and expanded to Seattle, Los Angeles and New York before pulling back and laying off 257 people in 2018. It shut down abruptly in January 2019 after raising about $125M, leaving some suppliers unpaid.

name: Beepi
one_liner: Peer-to-peer online marketplace for inspected used cars
story: Beepi inspected private sellers' cars and sold them online, raising about $150M at a peak valuation near $560M. Spending stayed high, sales to Fair.com and dealer group DGDG both collapsed, and it shut down in February 2017 with its parts sold to repay creditors.

name: Bird
one_liner: Dockless shared electric scooters rented by app
story: Bird became one of the fastest startups ever to reach a $1B valuation by dropping scooters on city sidewalks, reaching a $2.5B valuation in 2019. Scooters wore out fast and cities capped fleets; after a 2021 SPAC listing it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2023 to sell itself.

name: Lime
one_liner: Dockless shared e-scooters and e-bikes in cities worldwide
story: Lime raced Bird with the same dockless scooter model and hit a $2.4B valuation in 2019. In the 2020 crash Uber led a $170M rescue round at a reported $510M valuation and handed Lime its Jump bike unit; Lime cut costs and kept operating while Bird went bankrupt.

name: Jawbone
one_liner: Maker of Bluetooth headsets, Jambox speakers and UP fitness trackers
story: Jawbone raised around $1B and was valued at about $3B on headsets, speakers and UP fitness bands. Faulty trackers, costly lawsuits with Fitbit and competition from Fitbit and Apple Watch led to a down round in 2016 and liquidation in July 2017.

name: Pebble
one_liner: Kickstarter-funded e-paper smartwatch
story: Pebble set Kickstarter records in 2012 and 2015 with its smartwatch preorders, but struggled after Apple Watch launched and smartwatch demand fell short. Fitbit bought its software assets and hired staff in late 2016; Fitbit's filing showed it paid $23M, far below earlier reports of $40M.

name: Yik Yak
one_liner: Anonymous, location-based message board popular on college campuses
story: Yik Yak spread across US campuses in 2014 and raised about $73M at a valuation reported near $400M. Bullying and threats led schools to ban it, a move away from anonymity alienated users, and in 2017 it shut down after Square paid about $1M to hire its engineers.

name: Secret
one_liner: App for sharing anonymous posts with friends and friends-of-friends
story: Secret went viral in Silicon Valley in 2014 as an anonymous gossip app, raising about $35M at a valuation over $100M. Engagement fell and bullying concerns grew, and in April 2015 its founder shut it down and returned remaining cash to investors.

name: Color Labs
one_liner: Proximity-based photo-sharing app that raised $41M before launch
story: Color raised $41M before launching an app that showed photos from strangers nearby, one of the largest pre-launch raises of its era. Users found the app confusing and empty, a pivot failed, and Apple hired much of the team in 2012 while the app shut down.

name: Juicero
one_liner: Wi-Fi-connected juice press that squeezed proprietary produce packs
story: Juicero raised about $120M from investors including Google Ventures to sell a $699 connected juice press with subscription produce packs. In April 2017 Bloomberg showed the packs could be squeezed by hand just as well, and the company shut down that September.

name: Theranos
one_liner: Claimed to run hundreds of lab tests from a finger-prick of blood
story: Theranos raised more than $700M at a valuation of about $9B on claims its Edison device could run broad lab tests from a drop of blood, and rolled out testing in Walgreens stores. A 2015 Wall Street Journal investigation showed the technology did not work; the company dissolved in 2018 and founder Elizabeth Holmes was convicted of fraud in 2022.

name: Solyndra
one_liner: Maker of cylindrical thin-film solar panels
story: Solyndra built a factory for novel cylindrical solar panels backed by a $535M federal loan guarantee. Falling silicon prices and cheap Chinese panels undercut its costs, and it filed for bankruptcy in September 2011, laying off about 1,100 workers and becoming a political scandal.

name: Quibi
one_liner: Mobile-only streaming service of premium 10-minute shows
story: Jeffrey Katzenberg and Meg Whitman raised $1.75B to make Hollywood-quality shows in 'quick bites' for phones only, with no sharing or TV casting at launch. It launched in April 2020 just as lockdowns kept people at home, signups stalled against free TikTok and YouTube, and it shut down after about six months in December 2020.

name: Zume
one_liner: Pizza delivery company that used robots and ovens in moving trucks
story: Zume made pizzas with robots and baked them in ovens inside delivery trucks, then took $375M from SoftBank in 2018 at a reported $2.25B valuation. The pizza oven-trucks never worked well enough, so in January 2020 it stopped making pizza, cut half its staff and pivoted to compostable food packaging, before shutting down and liquidating in June 2023 after raising about $445M.

name: Katerra
one_liner: Tech-driven construction company that tried to own the whole building supply chain
story: Katerra tried to vertically integrate construction, from design to its own factories for building components, raising about $2B mostly from SoftBank. It expanded factories and acquisitions faster than it could deliver projects profitably, and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in June 2021.

name: Convoy
one_liner: Digital freight brokerage matching shippers with truckers by app
story: Convoy used software to match shippers and truckers, backed by investors including Jeff Bezos, and raised $260M at a $3.8B valuation in April 2022. A freight recession crushed brokerage margins and capital dried up; it shut down in October 2023, and Flexport bought its technology but not its liabilities.

name: Olive AI
one_liner: AI 'digital workforce' automating hospital billing and admin tasks
story: Olive raised about $852M, more than any health IT startup before it, to automate hospital revenue-cycle work, hitting a $4B valuation in 2021. Its products spread across too many tasks without delivering consistent results, and after failing to raise more it sold two units to Waystar and Humata Health and shut down on October 31, 2023.

name: Fast
one_liner: One-click checkout button for online stores
story: Fast raised a $102M Series B led by Stripe in 2021 to sell a one-click checkout, then hired aggressively and spent heavily on marketing. The Information reported it made only about $600,000 in revenue that year; unable to raise again, it shut down in April 2022 and Affirm offered jobs to most of its engineers.

name: Argo AI
one_liner: Self-driving technology company backed by Ford and Volkswagen
story: Argo got a $1B commitment from Ford in 2017 and $2.6B in cash and assets from Volkswagen, reaching a reported $7.25B valuation. When it failed to attract outside investors and Ford decided fully driverless cars were too far off to pay back, both backers pulled out and Argo shut down in October 2022; Ford took a $2.7B write-down.

name: Humane
one_liner: Screenless AI Pin wearable meant to replace the smartphone
story: Founded by ex-Apple staff, Humane raised more than $230M and launched its $699 AI Pin in 2024 to poor reviews about heat, battery and slow answers. It reportedly sold about 10,000 units against a 100,000 goal; after seeking a $750M-$1B sale, it sold its software, patents and most staff to HP for $116M in February 2025 and bricked the pins.

name: Forward
one_liner: Tech-heavy membership primary care that pivoted to self-serve 'CarePod' kiosks
story: Ex-Google executive Adrian Aoun built Forward as a $149-a-month high-tech doctor's office, then bet on CarePods, booths where patients ran their own checkups; early pods reportedly cost over $1M each to build. Reported funding ranges from $400M to about $657M; it closed all locations and its app with no notice in November 2024, cutting nearly 200 jobs.

name: Inflection AI
one_liner: AI lab behind the Pi personal assistant chatbot
story: Founded by DeepMind co-founder Mustafa Suleyman and Reid Hoffman, Inflection raised about $1.5B, including $1.3B in 2023 from Microsoft and Nvidia, to build the Pi chatbot. Unable to compete with OpenAI and Google on cost, in March 2024 it let Microsoft hire its founders and most staff and pay about $650M to license its models, a 'reverse acquihire' later probed by the FTC and UK CMA.

name: Character.AI
one_liner: Chatbots that role-play as celebrities, fictional characters and companions
story: Ex-Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas built Character.AI into one of the most-used consumer AI apps and raised $150M at a $1B valuation in 2023. In August 2024 Google paid a reported $2.7B, mostly as a non-exclusive license fee, and rehired the founders into DeepMind, while the remaining company kept running the app.

name: Adept
one_liner: AI agents that operate software on a user's behalf
story: Adept was founded by ex-OpenAI and Google researchers to build AI agents that click and type in software for users, raising about $415M. In June 2024 Amazon hired CEO David Luan, four co-founders and a large share of staff and took a non-exclusive license to its technology, with terms undisclosed.

name: Covariant
one_liner: AI foundation models for warehouse picking robots
story: Founded by Berkeley robotics researchers Pieter Abbeel, Peter Chen and Rocky Duan, Covariant built AI that let warehouse robots pick unfamiliar items, last valued at a reported $625M. In August 2024 Amazon hired its three founders and about a quarter of staff and licensed its models, with terms undisclosed.

name: Windsurf (Codeium)
one_liner: AI coding assistant and agentic code editor
story: Windsurf began as GPU startup Exafunction, pivoted to the Codeium coding assistant and raised $243M at a $1.25B valuation. A roughly $3B sale to OpenAI collapsed in July 2025; days later Google paid $2.4B in license fees and compensation to hire CEO Varun Mohan and key researchers, and Cognition bought the remaining company and product.

name: Sonder
one_liner: Tech-run apartment-hotel brand leasing whole buildings for short stays
story: Started in Montreal as Flatbook, Sonder signed long leases on apartment buildings and rented units like hotel rooms, going public via SPAC in 2022. Fixed lease costs weighed on it for years; after Marriott ended a 2024 licensing partnership on November 7, 2025, Sonder stopped operations immediately and filed for Chapter 7 liquidation, with some guests asked to leave on short notice.

name: Celsius Network
one_liner: Crypto lending platform paying high yields on customer deposits
story: Celsius promised retail customers high double-digit yields on crypto deposits and lent and traded the funds in risky strategies. When crypto prices crashed it froze withdrawals in June 2022 and filed for Chapter 11 a month later; founder Alex Mashinsky pleaded guilty to fraud and was sentenced to 12 years in prison in 2025.

name: BlockFi
one_liner: Crypto lender offering interest accounts and loans backed by bitcoin
story: BlockFi paid interest on crypto deposits and reached a $3B valuation in 2021, then paid $100M in early 2022 to settle SEC and state charges over its interest product. After losses tied to Three Arrows Capital it took a rescue credit line from FTX, and when FTX collapsed in November 2022 BlockFi filed for bankruptcy within weeks.

name: QuadrigaCX
one_liner: Canada's largest crypto exchange, until its founder died holding the keys
story: QuadrigaCX collapsed after founder Gerald Cotten died in India in December 2018, supposedly the only person with access to cold wallets holding customer crypto; about C$215M was owed to roughly 76,000 users. Ontario's securities regulator later found the wallets were mostly empty and that Cotten had run a fraud, trading and losing client funds and inventing balances.

name: Voyager Digital
one_liner: Toronto-listed crypto broker paying yield on customer deposits
story: Voyager lent customer crypto to firms including hedge fund Three Arrows Capital, which defaulted on a loan of roughly $650M in 2022. It filed for bankruptcy in July 2022; a sale to FTX died with FTX's collapse and a later deal with Binance.US also fell through, leaving it to liquidate.

name: Coinbase
one_liner: Regulated US exchange for buying and holding crypto
story: Coinbase, a Y Combinator company, made buying bitcoin simple and chose to work within US regulation while rival exchanges cut corners. It survived several crypto crashes and went public by direct listing in April 2021, closing its first day at a valuation of about $86B.

name: Stripe
one_liner: Developer-friendly API for accepting online payments
story: Irish brothers Patrick and John Collison built Stripe so developers could accept payments with a few lines of code. It reached a $95B valuation in 2021, raised $6.5B at a lower $50B valuation in 2023, and stayed private while letting employees sell shares in tender offers.

name: Mint
one_liner: Free app that pulled all your bank accounts into one budget view
story: Mint automatically synced users' bank and card accounts through an aggregator and categorized spending, while rival Wesabe asked users to upload data manually. Intuit bought Mint for $170M in 2009, about two years after launch; Intuit shut the app in 2024 and moved users to Credit Karma.

name: Wesabe
one_liner: Privacy-focused personal finance and budgeting site
story: Wesabe launched before Mint with a similar money-management idea but required more manual work from users, partly to protect privacy. Co-founder Marc Hedlund later wrote that Mint won because it was simply easier to use; Wesabe shut down in 2010, a year after Mint sold to Intuit.

name: Chime
one_liner: Fee-free mobile bank account with early paycheck access
story: Chime offered no-fee checking and early direct-deposit access through partner banks, earning mostly from card interchange fees. It hit a $25B private valuation in 2021 and went public in June 2025 at $27 a share, well below that private peak.

name: Frank
one_liner: App to help students fill out federal college financial-aid forms
story: JPMorgan Chase bought Frank for $175M in 2021 based on claims of more than 4 million users, while the real figure was closer to 300,000; prosecutors said founder Charlie Javice had a fake customer list generated. JPMorgan shut the product, a jury convicted Javice of fraud in 2025, and she was sentenced to more than seven years in prison.

name: Kik Interactive
one_liner: Anonymous messaging app popular with teens that bet on its own crypto token
story: Founded by University of Waterloo students, Kik grew to hundreds of millions of registered users and took $50M from Tencent at a $1B valuation in 2015. Losing ground to WhatsApp and Snapchat, it raised about $100M selling its Kin crypto token in 2017; the SEC sued over the sale in 2019, and Kik sold the messenger app to MediaLab that year.

name: Shopify
one_liner: Software that lets any merchant set up an online store
story: Tobias Lütke built Shopify after finding existing e-commerce software too poor for his own snowboard shop. It listed in New York and Toronto in May 2015, raising $131M, and grew into Canada's most valuable tech company as small merchants moved online.

name: Wealthsimple
one_liner: Canadian app for automated investing, trading, crypto and tax filing
story: Wealthsimple started as a low-fee robo-advisor backed by Power Corporation and expanded into commission-free trading, crypto and tax filing for Canadians. A C$750M round in 2021 valued it at C$5B (about US$4B), and it pulled out of the US and UK to focus on Canada.

name: Hopper
one_liner: Mobile travel app that predicts when flight and hotel prices will drop
story: Hopper spent years building price-prediction data before launching a mobile-only booking app, then made money selling add-ons like price freezes and flexible cancellation. A 2021 round valued it at about $3.5B.

name: Cohere
one_liner: Enterprise-focused large language models
story: Co-founded by Aidan Gomez, a co-author of the Transformer paper, Cohere sold models to enterprises that wanted private deployments rather than chasing consumers. Unlike Inflection and Adept, it kept raising independently, reaching a $6.8B valuation in 2025.

name: Element AI
one_liner: Montreal AI lab co-founded by Yoshua Bengio selling AI to enterprises
story: Element AI raised a record US$102M Series A in 2017 and about US$151M more in 2019 to sell AI products to big companies. Enterprise demand was early and projects looked like costly consulting; ServiceNow bought it in late 2020 for a price reported well below the more than US$250M raised.

name: Wattpad
one_liner: Social platform where millions write and read serialized fiction
story: Wattpad built a huge community of mostly young readers and writers sharing serialized stories, then turned hit stories into books, films and TV. South Korea's Naver bought it in 2021 for about US$600M.

name: Tesla
one_liner: Electric carmaker that started with an expensive sports car and moved down-market
story: Tesla sold the high-priced Roadster first to fund cheaper cars later, nearly running out of money in 2008 before Elon Musk and Daimler kept it alive. A $465M Department of Energy loan and a June 2010 IPO that raised $226M at about $1.7B funded the Model S, while most EV startups of the era failed.

name: Rivian
one_liner: Electric pickup, SUV and delivery-van maker backed by Amazon
story: Rivian spent a decade in quiet development before Amazon led a $700M round in 2019 and ordered 100,000 electric delivery vans, giving it a guaranteed customer. Its November 2021 IPO raised about $11.9B, one of the largest US listings ever, though its value fell sharply as production ramped slowly.

name: Nikola
one_liner: Hydrogen and battery-electric semi-truck startup
story: Nikola went public via SPAC in June 2020 and was briefly worth more than Ford before a Hindenburg Research report showed a promotional video of its truck had been rolled down a hill. Founder Trevor Milton was convicted of fraud in 2022 (and later pardoned in 2025), and the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February 2025.

name: Lordstown Motors
one_liner: Electric pickup maker in a former GM plant in Ohio
story: Lordstown bought a former GM plant and went public via SPAC in 2020 on claims of strong preorders for its Endurance pickup, which a short seller said were largely non-binding. It sold the plant to Foxconn in 2022, built only a handful of trucks, and filed for bankruptcy in June 2023 while suing Foxconn over a failed investment deal.

name: Fisker Inc.
one_liner: Asset-light EV maker that outsourced production of its Ocean SUV
story: Designer Henrik Fisker's second EV company went public via SPAC in 2020 and had Magna build its Ocean SUV, which reached customers in 2023 with software and quality problems. Sales and cash fell short and it filed for Chapter 11 in June 2024, about a decade after his first company, Fisker Automotive, also went bankrupt.

name: Canoo
one_liner: EV startup building pod-shaped vans on a 'skateboard' platform
story: Canoo went public via SPAC in December 2020 promising subscription EVs on a modular platform, then churned through strategies and executives without reaching volume production. It filed for Chapter 7 liquidation in January 2025.

name: Uber
one_liner: App to hail a ride from a nearby driver
story: Uber began as a black-car service and expanded into cheap peer-to-peer rides after Sidecar and Lyft proved drivers with personal cars would work, raising tens of billions to subsidize growth worldwide. It retreated from China, Russia and Southeast Asia by selling to local rivals, went public in May 2019 at $82.4B, and turned consistently profitable years later.

name: Hyperloop One
one_liner: Company developing near-vacuum tube 'hyperloop' transport
story: Inspired by Elon Musk's 2013 hyperloop paper, the company (renamed Virgin Hyperloop after Richard Branson invested) ran the first passenger test in a tube in Las Vegas in 2020. No government signed a full route, a pivot to cargo did not help, and it shut down at the end of 2023.

name: Cruise
one_liner: Self-driving robotaxi startup bought by General Motors
story: Y Combinator company Cruise started with highway autopilot kits and was bought by GM in 2016 in a deal reported at around $1B, a great outcome for its founders. Under GM it launched driverless robotaxis in San Francisco, but after a 2023 crash in which a car dragged a pedestrian, its permit was suspended and GM shut the robotaxi program in December 2024.

name: Aurora Innovation
one_liner: Self-driving software company focused on long-haul trucks
story: Founded by veterans of Google's, Tesla's and Uber's self-driving efforts, Aurora absorbed Uber's autonomy unit in 2020 and went public via SPAC in 2021 at about $11B. It focused on highway trucking rather than city robotaxis and began driverless commercial runs in Texas in 2025, while Argo shut down and GM closed Cruise.

name: Starsky Robotics
one_liner: Autonomous trucks with remote human drivers for tricky stretches
story: Starsky combined highway autonomy with remote teleoperators and in 2019 ran a truck with no one on board on a Florida highway. Its founder later wrote that investors wanted flashier AI progress than safety work and that the technology was further off than the industry claimed; it shut down in March 2020.

name: Proterra
one_liner: Maker of battery-electric transit buses and EV batteries
story: Proterra was a leader in US electric transit buses and went public via SPAC in 2021. Fixed-price bus contracts signed before supply-chain inflation turned unprofitable, and it filed for Chapter 11 in August 2023, selling its units separately.

name: KiOR
one_liner: Converted wood chips into renewable crude oil
story: Khosla Ventures-backed KiOR went public in 2011 promising cheap gasoline and diesel from wood biomass. Its Mississippi plant produced far less fuel than planned at uncompetitive cost, and it filed for bankruptcy in November 2014.

name: Teledesic
one_liner: Planned low-earth-orbit satellite internet constellation backed by Craig McCaw and Bill Gates
story: Teledesic planned hundreds of low-orbit satellites to deliver global broadband, essentially Starlink two decades early, with backing from Craig McCaw and Bill Gates. Launch costs were far too high, Iridium's 1999 bankruptcy scared investors, and Teledesic suspended its satellite work in 2002.

name: Virgin Orbit
one_liner: Launched small satellites from a rocket dropped by a converted Boeing 747
story: Spun out of Richard Branson's Virgin Galactic, Virgin Orbit air-launched small rockets from a 747 and went public via SPAC in late 2021. Launch volumes stayed low against SpaceX's cheap rideshare missions, its first UK launch failed in January 2023, and it filed for bankruptcy that April.

name: SpaceX
one_liner: Reusable rockets and the Starlink satellite internet network
story: SpaceX's first three Falcon 1 launches failed and it nearly ran out of money in 2008 before the fourth reached orbit and NASA awarded it a $1.6B cargo contract. Reusable rockets cut launch costs, and Starlink achieved the satellite-internet idea that Teledesic and Iridium could not; a December 2024 share sale valued it at about $350B.

name: WeWork
one_liner: Coworking company that leased offices long-term and rented desks short-term
story: WeWork signed long leases and rented desks short-term, pitching itself as a tech company; SoftBank's January 2019 investment valued it at $47B. Its 2019 IPO filing exposed huge losses and governance problems, the IPO was pulled and founder Adam Neumann ousted; after a 2021 SPAC listing at about $9B it filed for Chapter 11 in November 2023, wiping out shareholders before emerging under new owners in 2024.

name: Opendoor
one_liner: Buys homes instantly with algorithmic offers and resells them
story: Opendoor made instant cash offers on homes and resold them, going public in December 2020 through Chamath Palihapitiya's SPAC at about $4.8B. When Zillow tried the same model it shut its iBuying arm in 2021 after big losses, while Opendoor kept going despite heavy losses of its own in the housing downturn.

name: Facebook
one_liner: Real-identity social network that started at Harvard
story: Facebook launched at Harvard in 2004 and expanded one college at a time, so each campus reached critical mass before the next opened, while Friendster's servers buckled and MySpace filled with spam. It raised $16B in its May 2012 IPO at a $104B valuation.

name: Instagram
one_liner: Mobile photo-sharing app with filters
story: Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger stripped their check-in app Burbn down to one feature, photo sharing with filters, and launched on iPhone in 2010. About 18 months later, with 13 employees, Facebook bought it for $1B in April 2012, days after it raised at a $500M valuation, the same era in which Color burned $41M on a similar idea.

name: Myspace
one_liner: Customizable-profile social network popular with musicians
story: Myspace became the most visited US social network by letting anyone customize profiles and by courting bands, and News Corp bought its parent Intermix for $580M in 2005. Spam, clutter and an ad-heavy redesign pushed users to Facebook, and News Corp sold Myspace for about $35M in 2011.

name: Friendster
one_liner: The first mainstream social network of friends-of-friends
story: Friendster grew to millions of users in 2003 and reportedly turned down a $30M offer from Google, then raised $13M from Kleiner Perkins and Benchmark. Pages took so long to load that US users left for Myspace and Facebook while its board focused elsewhere; it survived on Asian users and was sold to Malaysia's MOL Global in 2009 before shutting in 2015.

name: Groupon
one_liner: Daily group-buying discounts at local businesses
story: Groupon pivoted from a collective-action site called The Point into daily deals and became one of the fastest-growing companies ever, turning down a reported $6B offer from Google in 2010. It raised $700M in a November 2011 IPO at about $12.7B, but merchant fatigue and copycats sent the stock far lower within a few years.

name: LivingSocial
one_liner: Daily-deals rival to Groupon backed by Amazon
story: LivingSocial was Groupon's closest US rival and took a $175M investment from Amazon in 2010, reaching a multibillion-dollar valuation. As the daily-deals boom faded it shrank through layoffs, and Groupon bought it in 2016 for an undisclosed price far below its peak.

name: Digg
one_liner: Social news site where users voted stories to the front page
story: Digg was one of the web's biggest traffic sources in the late 2000s and held acquisition talks with Google. A 2010 redesign that favored publishers over its community triggered a user revolt to Reddit, and in 2012 its remains sold to Betaworks for about $500,000.

name: Gawker Media
one_liner: Network of gossip and tech blogs including Gawker.com
story: Gawker Media built a profitable network of blogs without much outside funding. A jury awarded Hulk Hogan $140M in 2016 over Gawker's publication of his sex tape in a lawsuit secretly funded by Peter Thiel; the company went bankrupt and sold its sites to Univision for $135M, shutting Gawker.com.

name: Aereo
one_liner: Streamed over-the-air TV to subscribers using thousands of tiny antennas
story: Backed by Barry Diller's IAC, Aereo assigned each subscriber a dime-sized antenna to stream broadcast channels, arguing it did not need to pay networks. In June 2014 the US Supreme Court ruled against it in ABC v. Aereo, and it filed for bankruptcy that November.

name: Grooveshark
one_liner: Free on-demand music streaming built on user-uploaded songs
story: Grooveshark let users upload and stream almost any song free, without licenses from most major labels. After years of label lawsuits and a court finding of liability, it settled and shut down in April 2015, while licensed services like Spotify and Pandora grew.

name: Rdio
one_liner: Licensed music streaming service from the founders of Skype
story: Rdio launched a well-reviewed licensed streaming service before Spotify reached the US, but struggled with marketing and royalty costs as Spotify grew. It filed for bankruptcy in November 2015 and Pandora bought its key assets for $75M.

name: Pandora
one_liner: Personalized internet radio built on the Music Genome Project
story: Pandora nearly died after the dot-com crash, with dozens of employees working unpaid for months before new funding arrived in 2004. Its licensed radio model avoided the lawsuits that killed Napster and Grooveshark; it went public in 2011 at about $2.6B and SiriusXM bought it for $3.5B in 2019.

name: MoviePass
one_liner: Monthly subscription for going to the movies in theaters
story: After data firm Helios and Matheson took control in 2017, MoviePass cut its price to $9.95 a month for a movie a day while paying theaters full ticket price, and subscribers jumped past 3 million. Losses exploded, the service shut down in 2019 and its parent filed for bankruptcy in early 2020; a co-founder later bought back the brand and relaunched it.

name: Fyre Media
one_liner: Celebrity-booking app that promoted the luxury Fyre Festival
story: Billy McFarland and Ja Rule's Fyre Media marketed a luxury music festival in the Bahamas with influencer posts, but guests in April 2017 found disaster-relief tents and cheese sandwiches. McFarland pleaded guilty to defrauding investors and ticket buyers and was sentenced to six years in prison.

name: OnLive
one_liner: Streamed high-end video games from the cloud to any screen
story: OnLive launched cloud gaming in 2010, running games on its servers and streaming them to players, but needed costly dedicated hardware per concurrent user while few people subscribed. In 2012 it restructured through an assignment for the benefit of creditors that wiped out investors, and Sony bought its patents and shut it in 2015.

name: Gaikai
one_liner: Cloud streaming of instant-play video game demos
story: Gaikai streamed playable game demos inside websites and sold the service to publishers rather than charging consumers. Sony bought it for $380M in 2012, the same year rival OnLive collapsed, and used its technology for PlayStation Now.

name: Ouya
one_liner: $99 Android-based TV game console funded on Kickstarter
story: Ouya raised about $8.6M in Kickstarter preorders in 2012 for a cheap open console, one of the platform's biggest campaigns. Players bought few games and developers earned little; Razer acquired its software and team in 2015 and shut the store in 2019.

name: General Magic
one_liner: Apple spinout that designed a smartphone-like handheld communicator in the early 1990s
story: Former Apple engineers founded General Magic to build Magic Cap, a touchscreen communicator OS, and its 1995 IPO doubled on day one. Devices launched before cheap wireless data existed and sold poorly; after a pivot to voice services it liquidated in 2002, while alumni went on to lead the iPhone and Android projects.

name: Fab.com
one_liner: Flash-sale site for design products
story: Fab pivoted from a social network into design flash sales in 2011 and grew so fast it reached a roughly $1B valuation, expanding into Europe and its own inventory. Growth stalled and costs ballooned, and after several pivots it was sold to manufacturing firm PCH in 2015 for a small fraction of the money raised.

name: uBiome
one_liner: Gut microbiome testing kits sold to consumers and billed to insurers
story: uBiome started with crowdfunding for at-home microbiome kits and raised an $83M Series C in 2018 at a $600M valuation. After an FBI raid in April 2019 over its insurance billing practices it went bankrupt that year, and its co-founders were later indicted on fraud charges.

name: Pear Therapeutics
one_liner: FDA-authorized prescription apps for addiction and insomnia
story: Pear won the first FDA authorization for a prescription digital therapeutic, reSET for substance use disorder, in 2017 and went public via SPAC in 2021. Insurers rarely paid for the apps, so revenue stayed small, and it filed for bankruptcy in April 2023 and sold its assets for a few million dollars.

name: Cue Health
one_liner: At-home molecular COVID-19 test reader
story: Cue Health's home molecular COVID test sold heavily during the pandemic and it went public in 2021. When COVID testing demand collapsed and the FDA issued a warning letter about its test, it could not replace the revenue and shut down in 2024.

name: Moderna
one_liner: mRNA medicines platform company
story: Created by Flagship Pioneering, Moderna raised billions privately to build an mRNA platform before any product was approved, then raised $604M in a December 2018 IPO, the largest biotech IPO at the time. Its platform let it design a COVID-19 vaccine within days in 2020, turning it into one of the pandemic's biggest winners.

name: Kite Pharma
one_liner: CAR-T cell therapies for blood cancers
story: Founded by serial entrepreneur Arie Belldegrun, Kite licensed CAR-T technology from the National Cancer Institute and went public in 2014. Strong lymphoma trial results led Gilead to buy it for $11.9B in 2017, just before its first therapy was approved.

name: Oscar Health
one_liner: Tech-first health insurer selling individual plans
story: Oscar launched in 2013 to sell easy-to-use health plans on the new Affordable Care Act exchanges. It raised $1.4B in a March 2021 IPO at about $7.9B, then lost much of that value before reaching profitability years later.

name: Lemonade
one_liner: App-based renters and home insurance with an AI claims bot
story: Lemonade sold renters insurance to young customers through a chatbot and promised to give unclaimed premiums to charity. Its July 2020 IPO raised $319M and more than doubled on day one; it later bought struggling car insurer Metromile.

name: Metromile
one_liner: Pay-per-mile car insurance using a plug-in tracking device
story: Metromile charged drivers by the mile using a device in their car and went public via SPAC in early 2021. High claims losses and a crashing share price led it to sell to Lemonade in an all-stock deal announced at about $500M, far below its SPAC valuation, which closed in 2022.

name: Zenefits
one_liner: Free HR software paid for by health-insurance broker commissions
story: Zenefits gave small businesses free HR software and earned broker commissions on their health insurance, reaching a $4.5B valuation in 2015. In 2016 it emerged that founder Parker Conrad had built a tool to let staff skip California's required broker-licensing training; he resigned, its valuation was cut, and TriNet bought it in 2022.

name: Rippling
one_liner: Unified HR, payroll and IT platform for businesses
story: After being pushed out of Zenefits, Parker Conrad started Rippling to tackle the same small-business HR market, this time charging for software and building payroll and IT tools on a single employee database. It reached a $13.5B valuation in 2024, several times what Zenefits was worth at its peak.

name: Atrium
one_liner: Tech-enabled law firm for startups from Twitch co-founder Justin Kan
story: Justin Kan's Atrium paired an in-house law firm with software to make startup legal work cheaper and faster, raising $75.5M. Legal work proved hard to automate, it laid off its lawyers in early 2020 to pivot to advisory services, and shut down weeks later.

name: Casetext
one_liner: AI legal research and the CoCounsel lawyer assistant
story: Casetext spent a decade building legal research tools, then used early access to GPT-4 to launch CoCounsel, an AI legal assistant, in 2023. Months later Thomson Reuters bought it for $650M in cash.

name: Palantir
one_liner: Data-integration software for intelligence agencies, militaries and enterprises
story: Co-founded by Peter Thiel with early backing from the CIA's venture arm In-Q-Tel, Palantir sold to government agencies for years when most VCs avoided the sector. It went public by direct listing in September 2020 at about $21B and later became one of the most valuable US software companies.

name: Knewton
one_liner: Adaptive-learning engine that personalized digital coursework
story: Knewton raised well over $100M promising an adaptive-learning engine that would personalize education, licensed through publishers like Pearson. The publisher partnerships disappointed, a pivot to its own courseware did not grow fast enough, and Wiley bought its assets in 2019 for a reported fraction of the money raised.

name: Edmodo
one_liner: Facebook-style social network for teachers and students
story: Edmodo spread through schools as a free classroom network adopted teacher by teacher, reaching tens of millions of users. China's NetDragon bought it for $137.5M in 2018, but it never found a strong business model and was shut down in 2022 after Google Classroom took over.

name: IronNet
one_liner: Network cyber-defense company founded by a former NSA director
story: Founded by former NSA director Gen. Keith Alexander, IronNet sold collective cyber-defense software and went public via SPAC in 2021. Sales lagged its forecasts and losses mounted, and it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2023.

name: CrowdStrike
one_liner: Cloud-native endpoint security platform
story: CrowdStrike delivered endpoint protection from the cloud while incumbents sold on-premise antivirus, and gained fame investigating high-profile breaches. Its June 2019 IPO raised $612M at about $6.7B and it grew into one of the largest security companies.

name: Duo Security
one_liner: Easy two-factor authentication for businesses
story: Built in Ann Arbor, Michigan, Duo made two-factor login simple enough for any company to deploy. Cisco bought it for $2.35B in cash in 2018, one of the largest exits for a Midwest startup.

name: GitHub
one_liner: Hosting and collaboration platform for code built on Git
story: GitHub's founders ran it profitably without venture money for four years before taking a $100M Series A from Andreessen Horowitz in 2012. It became the default home for open-source code, and Microsoft bought it for $7.5B in stock in 2018.

name: RethinkDB
one_liner: Open-source realtime JSON database
story: RethinkDB built a well-loved open-source database but struggled to get developers to pay, while MongoDB won the market. It shut down in 2016; co-founder Slava Akhmechet later wrote that it chased technical correctness over what the market wanted, and the code was handed to the Linux Foundation.

name: Kite
one_liner: AI-powered code completion for programmers
story: Kite offered machine-learning code completion years before ChatGPT and gained hundreds of thousands of users. Its founder said in a 2022 farewell post that the AI was not yet good enough to change how developers work and that developers would not pay; it shut down months before AI coding tools like Cursor took off.

name: Slack
one_liner: Team messaging app born from a failed online game
story: Stewart Butterfield's company Tiny Speck, started in Vancouver, built the online game Glitch, which failed in 2012; its internal chat tool became Slack. Slack spread team by team, went public by direct listing in 2019 and was bought by Salesforce for $27.7B in 2021.

name: Neeva
one_liner: Ad-free, subscription search engine from Google's former ads chief
story: Former Google ads head Sridhar Ramaswamy built Neeva as a private, ad-free search engine and added AI answers early. Few users paid to switch from Google, it shut its consumer search in 2023 and Snowflake acquired the company; Ramaswamy became Snowflake's CEO in 2024.

name: MosaicML
one_liner: Tools for companies to train their own large language models cheaply
story: MosaicML helped companies train their own language models efficiently and released open models just as generative AI took off. Databricks bought it for $1.3B in June 2023, about two years after its founding.

name: OpenAI
one_liner: AI lab behind ChatGPT and the GPT models
story: OpenAI began as a nonprofit research lab in 2015, created a capped-profit arm to raise money from Microsoft, and launched ChatGPT in November 2022, the fastest-growing consumer app of its time. A 2025 funding round led by SoftBank valued it at $300B, and a share sale later that year reportedly valued it at $500B.

name: Anysphere (Cursor)
one_liner: Maker of Cursor, an AI-first code editor
story: Founded by four MIT students, Anysphere forked VS Code into Cursor and built AI editing directly into the editor, arriving just as models became good enough. It grew to a $9.9B valuation by mid-2025 with reported later rounds far higher, while earlier AI coding startup Kite had shut down in 2022 and rival Windsurf was split up.

name: Scale AI
one_liner: Human-labeled training data for AI models
story: Y Combinator company Scale AI supplied labeled data first to self-driving companies and then to AI labs, reaching a $13.8B valuation in 2024. In June 2025 Meta invested about $14.3B for 49% of the company and hired founder Alexandr Wang to lead its superintelligence effort, the largest of the 'acquihire-style' AI deals.

name: Airbnb
one_liner: Marketplace for renting rooms and homes from locals
story: Airbnb's founders kept the company alive in 2008 by selling novelty cereal boxes before joining Y Combinator and raising $600K from Sequoia. COVID nearly wiped out bookings in 2020, but after $1B in emergency financing it went public that December, raising $3.5B at about $47B and roughly doubling on day one.

name: DoorDash
one_liner: Restaurant delivery marketplace
story: Stanford students started DoorDash by delivering from Palo Alto restaurants themselves, then focused on suburbs that rivals ignored. Unlike Sprig and Munchery, it never cooked food, only delivered it; it went public in December 2020 raising $3.37B and became the US delivery leader.

name: Instacart
one_liner: Same-day grocery delivery by personal shoppers from existing stores
story: Instacart revived Webvan's idea without warehouses or trucks, sending gig shoppers into existing supermarkets and partnering with grocers. Pandemic demand pushed its private valuation to $39B in 2021, and it went public in September 2023 at about $9.9B.

name: Gopuff
one_liner: Delivers snacks and essentials from its own micro-warehouses in about 30 minutes
story: Two Drexel students started Gopuff delivering snacks to college students, owning inventory in small warehouses and charging a delivery fee, which gave it retail margins that Kozmo never had. It grew slowly for years before raising $1.15B at a $15B valuation in 2021.

name: Chewy
one_liner: Online pet food and supply retailer known for customer service
story: Chewy sold the same heavy pet food that sank Pets.com, but a decade later with cheaper shipping, repeat 'Autoship' subscriptions and obsessive customer service. PetSmart bought it for $3.35B in 2017, then the largest e-commerce acquisition ever, and Chewy went public in 2019.

name: Carvana
one_liner: Buy a used car online and pick it up from a car vending machine
story: Spun out of used-car dealer DriveTime, Carvana owned and reconditioned its inventory rather than matching private sellers like Beepi, and it went public in 2017 raising $225M. It nearly collapsed under debt in 2022, then cut costs and recovered.

name: Dollar Shave Club
one_liner: Razor blades by monthly subscription
story: Dollar Shave Club launched in 2012 with a cheap, profane YouTube video that went viral and brought thousands of subscribers in its first days. It undercut Gillette's pricing, and Unilever bought it for a reported $1B in 2016.

name: Beyond Meat
one_liner: Plant-based burgers and sausages sold in grocery stores and restaurants
story: Beyond Meat placed plant-based burgers in the grocery meat aisle and raised $240M in a May 2019 IPO that jumped 163% on day one, one of the best debuts in years. Demand faded in later years and the stock fell far below its IPO price.

name: The Climate Corporation
one_liner: Weather data and insurance tools for farmers
story: Ex-Google employees started WeatherBill to sell weather insurance, then focused on farmers using weather and soil data. Monsanto bought it for about $930M in 2013, one of the first big agtech exits.

name: AppNexus
one_liner: Programmatic advertising exchange and ad-buying platform
story: AppNexus built one of the largest independent real-time ad exchanges as an alternative to Google's ad stack. AT&T bought it in 2018 for a reported $1.6B to build its own advertising business.

name: HubSpot
one_liner: Inbound marketing and CRM software for small and mid-size businesses
story: HubSpot popularized 'inbound marketing', teaching businesses to attract customers with content and selling them the software to do it. It went public in 2014 and grew into a large CRM platform for smaller companies.

name: Fitbit
one_liner: Clip-on and wrist fitness trackers
story: Fitbit won the fitness-tracker market against Jawbone with reliable devices and strong retail distribution, and raised $732M in a 2015 IPO. Apple Watch later squeezed it, and Google bought it for $2.1B in 2021.

name: Flexport
one_liner: Software-driven international freight forwarder
story: Flexport became a licensed freight forwarder and customs broker and ran it with modern software, booming during the 2021 shipping crunch to an $8B valuation in 2022. It survived the freight downturn that killed Convoy and bought Convoy's technology in 2023.

name: Essential Products
one_liner: Premium Android phone maker founded by Android co-creator Andy Rubin
story: Andy Rubin raised about $330M at a valuation near $1B to take on Apple and Samsung with the Essential Phone, launched in 2017. Sales were small, a planned follow-up was cancelled, and the company shut down in February 2020.

name: Jibo
one_liner: Expressive social robot for the home from MIT's Cynthia Breazeal
story: Jibo was crowdfunded in 2014 and shipped in 2017 at $899 after delays, by which time far cheaper Amazon Echo and Google Home speakers did more. The company's assets went to a lender in 2018, and when its servers were shut down the robots told owners goodbye.

name: Rethink Robotics
one_liner: Collaborative factory robots Baxter and Sawyer from iRobot's co-founder
story: Founded by iRobot co-founder Rodney Brooks, Rethink made friendly, cheap robots that could work beside people. Baxter was not precise enough for many factory tasks, rivals like Universal Robots won the market, and Rethink shut down in 2018 after an acquisition fell through.

name: Brandless
one_liner: Online store selling unbranded household goods at $3 each
story: Brandless launched in 2017 selling food and household items for $3 each without brand names, and took $240M from SoftBank's Vision Fund in 2018. Low prices on small orders left little margin after shipping, leadership churned, and it shut down in early 2020.

name: Bowery Farming
one_liner: Indoor vertical farms growing greens near cities
story: Bowery grew lettuce in automated indoor farms near East Coast cities, reaching a $2.3B valuation in 2021. Energy costs made its greens expensive to produce, crop problems hit its farms, and it shut down in November 2024.

name: AppHarvest
one_liner: Giant high-tech greenhouses growing tomatoes in Kentucky
story: AppHarvest promised to bring agtech jobs to Appalachia with huge greenhouses and went public via SPAC in early 2021. Crop yields and quality fell short and costs ran high, and it filed for Chapter 11 in July 2023.

name: Casper
one_liner: Direct-to-consumer mattress shipped in a box
story: Casper popularized mattresses shipped compressed in a box and hit a $1.1B private valuation in 2019, but dozens of copycats drove up ad costs. Its February 2020 IPO priced at about half that valuation, and it was taken private in early 2022 for about $300M.

name: Blue Apron
one_liner: Subscription meal kits with recipes and pre-portioned ingredients
story: Blue Apron led the US meal-kit boom and was valued at about $2B privately, but went public in 2017 at a cut price the week Amazon agreed to buy Whole Foods. High customer churn and marketing costs left it losing money, and Wonder Group bought it for $103M in 2023, while Germany's HelloFresh became the global leader.

name: Workday
one_liner: Cloud HR and finance software for large enterprises
story: PeopleSoft founder Dave Duffield and Aneel Bhusri started Workday after Oracle's hostile takeover of PeopleSoft, rebuilding HR software for the cloud. It went public in October 2012, raising about $637M, and became a standard for large-company HR systems.
